title: A Theory of Terrorist Targeting and State Military Response
text:
1 Theoretical Problem
States do not respond uniformly to terrorism. Some terrorist campaigns remain primarily matters for police, intelligence agencies, and courts, while others lead governments to mobilize or deploy military forces. Why does terrorist violence sometimes lead governments to cross this threshold?
We argue that terrorist targeting affects state responses through two distinct mechanisms:

Political mechanism: Different targets threaten governments in different ways, and the political meaning of those targets varies systematically across regime types. In democracies, violence against civilians can create intense public pressure on elected leaders to demonstrate that they are protecting the population. In autocracies, attacks against the military, police, and other coercive institutions can be especially threatening because these institutions constitute the organizational foundation of regime survival.
Informational mechanism: Governments do not observe terrorist organizational capacity perfectly. Terrorist organizations, however, know more about their own capabilities. Target selection and attack performance can therefore provide governments with information about the adversary they face. Successfully and repeatedly attacking well-protected security targets may require intelligence, trained personnel, logistics, weapons, organizational coordination, and the ability to evade state security services. Such attacks can consequently cause governments to revise upward their assessment of a terrorist organization’s capabilities.

These mechanisms are analytically distinct. Regime type determines how much political pressure a particular target generates, while organizational behavior provides information about terrorist capacity. The latter mechanism need not be regime-specific. An attack on a difficult military target can signal organizational capability to a democracy as well as an autocracy.
The argument can therefore be summarized as:
\[\text{Terrorist targeting} \longrightarrow \begin{pmatrix} \text{Regime-specific political pressure} \\ \text{Belief updating about terrorist capacity} \end{pmatrix} \longrightarrow \text{State response}\]
This distinction generates an important implication: security targeting can induce military action even in democracies. Democracies need not experience civilian attacks before turning to military force. If attacks against security institutions reveal that a terrorist organization poses a sufficiently serious security threat, military escalation can become rational even when the direct political pressure generated by security attacks is relatively modest.
At the same time, security targeting may have an especially pronounced effect in autocracies because the same attack can operate through both mechanisms simultaneously: it can reveal terrorist capability while also directly threatening institutions central to regime survival.
Below is the complete game tree corresponding to the sequence \(\text{Nature chooses } \theta \rightarrow \text{terrorist chooses } j \rightarrow \text{attack outcome } y \rightarrow \text{government updates beliefs} \rightarrow \text{government chooses } r\).

Figure 1: Extensive-form game tree of the Bayesian targeting and military escalation model. Nature draws organizational capacity θ ∈ {L, H}; Terrorist (T) selects target j ∈ {C, S}; outcome y is realized with probability Pr(y | j, θ); Government (G) updates belief μ_j(y) and selects response r ∈ {0, P, M}.








2 The Strategic Environment
Consider an interaction between a terrorist organization \(T\) and a government \(G\).
Governments face a basic informational problem. They know that terrorist organizations vary greatly in capability, but they cannot perfectly observe the capacity of the organization confronting them.
Let terrorist organizational capacity be: \[\theta \in \{L, H\},\] where \(L\) denotes a relatively low-capacity organization and \(H\) denotes a relatively high-capacity organization.
Nature draws the organization’s type. The terrorist organization observes its own type, but the government does not. Initially, the government believes that the probability that it confronts a high-capacity organization is: \[\Pr(\theta = H) = \pi.\] The quantity \(\pi\) is the government’s prior belief.
The terrorist organization then chooses a target: \[j \in \{C, S\},\] where:

\(C\) denotes civilian targets, and
\(S\) denotes state security targets, including military, police, intelligence, or other coercive institutions.

An attack then produces an observable outcome \(y\). This may incorporate whether the operation succeeds, casualties, penetration of defenses, weapon sophistication, or other observable characteristics of operational performance.
After observing the attack, the government updates its belief about terrorist capacity and chooses a response: \[r \in \{0, P, M\},\] where:

\(0\) represents continuation of a relatively limited response,
\(P\) represents intensified policing, intelligence, judicial, or internal-security measures, and
\(M\) represents military mobilization or deployment.

The sequence of play is therefore:
\[\text{Nature chooses } \theta \longrightarrow \text{Terrorist chooses } j \longrightarrow \text{Outcome } y \longrightarrow \text{Government updates beliefs} \longrightarrow \text{Government chooses } r\]
The appropriate solution concept is Perfect Bayesian Equilibrium: terrorist organizations choose targets anticipating government reactions, while governments respond optimally given what observed terrorist behavior leads them to believe about the organization.



3 Why Targets Have Different Political Meanings
The first mechanism concerns the political consequences of terrorism.
Let \(P_j^z\) denote the political pressure an attack against target \(j\) imposes on a government with regime type \(z\), where: \[z \in \{D, A\}\] denotes democracy (\(D\)) and autocracy (\(A\)).
The theoretical argument requires only two inequalities. For democracies: \[P_C^D > P_S^D.\]
Civilian attacks are particularly politically costly because democratic leaders are accountable to a broad public. Highly visible failures to protect citizens can generate electoral punishment, media scrutiny, demands for government action, and challenges from political opponents. This does not mean security attacks impose zero political costs on democracies; in general, \(P_S^D > 0\). The claim is comparative: an otherwise similar attack on civilians is expected to generate greater direct public-accountability pressure.
The corresponding relationship in autocracies is: \[P_S^A > P_C^A.\]
Autocratic political survival depends less directly on electoral accountability to the mass public and more heavily on maintaining control over institutions capable of coercion. Successful attacks against soldiers, police officers, military installations, or other coercive institutions can expose weakness, damage regime prestige, encourage challengers, or threaten institutions upon which regime survival depends. Again, the claim is comparative rather than absolute: civilian casualties can certainly matter to autocratic governments, but attacks against the coercive apparatus carry a distinctive regime-survival cost.

This political-pressure mechanism is deliberately separate from the informational mechanism developed next.



4 Terrorist Targeting as Information
Imagine two organizations. One consists of a small number of poorly trained militants with limited weapons and intelligence. The other possesses experienced personnel, logistical networks, reconnaissance capabilities, explosives expertise, and the ability to coordinate complex operations.
Both organizations may be physically capable of attacking an unprotected civilian gathering. They may not be equally capable of penetrating a defended military installation. This creates the possibility that target choice itself contains information.
Let the operational cost of attacking target \(j\) be \(c_j(\theta)\). The crucial assumption is not simply that security targets are costly, but that they are relatively more costly for weak organizations: \[c_S(L) - c_C(L) > c_S(H) - c_C(H).\]
This is a standard single-crossing condition. In ordinary language, the additional difficulty associated with moving from an accessible civilian target to a protected security target is greater for a weak organization than for a strong organization. Consequently, governments can rationally treat certain forms of security targeting as evidence of terrorist organizational capacity.



5 Target Hardness Matters
A binary distinction between “civilian” and “security” targets is nevertheless too crude. Shooting an individual police officer and penetrating a heavily defended military command facility are both attacks on security targets, but they reveal very different capabilities.
Let \(h_j \ge 0\) represent target hardness. One operational-cost function reflecting this is: \[c_j(\theta, h_j) = \frac{\kappa h_j}{\theta}, \quad \kappa > 0,\] where higher values of \(\theta\) represent greater organizational capability.
This gives:

\(\dfrac{\partial c_j}{\partial h_j} > 0\): harder targets cost more to attack.
\(\dfrac{\partial c_j}{\partial \theta} < 0\): greater organizational capacity makes demanding attacks easier.
\(\dfrac{\partial^2 c_j}{\partial h_j \partial \theta} < 0\): as targets become harder, organizational capacity becomes increasingly valuable.

Therefore, the theoretical argument is not simply that \(\text{security target} = \text{strong organization}\), but rather:

The informational content of security targeting increases with the capability required to attack the target.

An attack on an exposed police patrol may provide relatively little information about organizational capability, whereas repeated penetration of fortified military installations may provide considerably more.



6 Bayesian Updating
After observing an attack against target \(j\) with outcome \(y\), the government calculates the posterior probability: \[\mu(j, y) = \Pr(\theta = H \mid j, y).\]
By Bayes’ rule: \[\mu(j, y) = \frac{\pi \Pr(j, y \mid H)}{\pi \Pr(j, y \mid H) + (1 - \pi) \Pr(j, y \mid L)}.\]
The government begins with prior belief \(\pi\) and updates based on how likely the observed behavior would have been if it were facing a high-capacity organization rather than a low-capacity one. A security attack increases the government’s assessment of terrorist capability when: \[\frac{\Pr(S, y \mid H)}{\Pr(S, y \mid L)} > 1.\]
Expressed in terms of posterior odds: \[\frac{\mu(j, y)}{1 - \mu(j, y)} = \left( \frac{\pi}{1 - \pi} \right) \times \left( \frac{\Pr(j, y \mid H)}{\Pr(j, y \mid L)} \right),\] or: \[\text{Posterior odds} = \text{Prior odds} \times \text{Likelihood ratio}.\]
Targeting affects beliefs only to the extent that the observed behavior distinguishes capable organizations from incapable ones.



7 The Government’s Choice Between Policing and Military Action
Let \(L_G(r \mid j, y, z)\) denote the government’s expected loss from choosing response \(r\): \[L_G(r \mid j, y, z) = K_r^z + P_j^z l_r + \mu(j, y) D_H(r) + [1 - \mu(j, y)] D_L(r).\]
Each component captures a key operational or political factor:

Cost of the response (\(K_r^z\)): Military action requires personnel, money, administrative capacity, and political commitment: \[K_M^z > K_P^z > K_0^z.\] Absent a sufficiently serious threat, governments prefer cheaper instruments.
Residual political pressure (\(P_j^z l_r\)): The parameter \(l_r\) represents the fraction of political pressure that remains unresolved after response \(r\). Assuming military action demonstrates a stronger response than policing: \[l_M < l_P.\]
Expected future terrorist damage: A government that believes it confronts a high-capacity organization places greater weight on \(D_H(r)\). If military force is particularly effective against such organizations, increases in \(\mu(j, y)\) make military action more attractive.




8 When Does a Government Militarize?
To isolate the escalation threshold, compare intensified policing (\(P\)) with military action (\(M\)). Define:

\(\Delta K^z = K_M^z - K_P^z > 0\): the additional cost of military action.
\(\Delta l = l_P - l_M > 0\): the additional political pressure relieved through military escalation.
\(\Delta D_\theta = D_\theta(P) - D_\theta(M)\): the additional security benefit of using military force against type \(\theta\).

Assume \(\Delta D_H > \Delta D_L\): military action is particularly valuable when the adversary is highly capable. The government chooses military action over policing when: \[P_j^z \Delta l + \mu(j, y) \Delta D_H + [1 - \mu(j, y)] \Delta D_L \ge \Delta K^z.\]
The government militarizes when the combination of political pressure relieved by escalation and expected security benefits from military action exceeds the additional cost of using the military.
Notice that there are two independent channels pushing toward military escalation: \[\begin{aligned}
P_j^z \uparrow &\implies \text{Military action becomes more attractive (Political channel)} \\
\mu(j, y) \uparrow &\implies \text{Military action becomes more attractive (Informational channel)}
\end{aligned}\]



9 A Belief Threshold for Military Action
The military-response condition can be rearranged directly in terms of the government’s posterior belief. Military action occurs if: \[\mu(j, y) \ge \bar{\mu}_j^z,\] where: \[\bar{\mu}_j^z = \frac{\Delta K^z - P_j^z \Delta l - \Delta D_L}{\Delta D_H - \Delta D_L}.\]
The quantity \(\bar{\mu}_j^z\) is the government’s militarization threshold. If the posterior belief exceeds this cutoff, military escalation becomes preferable to internal policing.
Importantly: \[\frac{\partial \bar{\mu}_j^z}{\partial P_j^z} = - \frac{\Delta l}{\Delta D_H - \Delta D_L} < 0.\]
Greater political pressure lowers the evidentiary hurdle regarding terrorist capacity required to provoke military escalation. Political pressure and information are therefore mutually reinforcing rather than rival explanations.



10 Why Security Targeting Can Militarize Democracies
Consider a democratic government observing an attack on a security target. Its military-response condition is: \[P_S^D \Delta l + \mu(S, y) \Delta D_H + [1 - \mu(S, y)] \Delta D_L \ge \Delta K^D.\]
While \(P_C^D > P_S^D\), we do not assume \(P_S^D = 0\). More importantly, security targeting increases \(\mu(S, y)\). Consequently, even a democracy experiencing no civilian attacks can rationally militarize if attacks against security targets sufficiently heighten its assessment of terrorist capability.

Proposition 1 (Security-Induced Militarization in Democracies) A security-target attack can induce military escalation in a democracy even when security targets generate less direct political pressure than civilian targets. Military escalation occurs whenever: \[\mu(S, y) \ge \frac{\Delta K^D - P_S^D \Delta l - \Delta D_L}{\Delta D_H - \Delta D_L}.\]


Corollary 1 (Independent Sufficiency of the Informational Mechanism) Even in the extreme case where security attacks create zero direct political pressure (\(P_S^D = 0\)), a democracy militarizes whenever: \[\mu(S, y) \ge \frac{\Delta K^D - \Delta D_L}{\Delta D_H - \Delta D_L}.\]

This prevents the theoretical framework from falsely implying that democracies militarize only when civilians are victimized.



11 Why Security Targeting May Have a Stronger Effect in Autocracies
Now compare that democratic government with an autocracy. In an autocracy, \(P_S^A > P_S^D\), but the informational content of the attack persists (\(\mu(S, y) > 0\)). A sufficiently difficult security attack activates both mechanisms simultaneously:
\[\text{Security targeting} \longrightarrow \begin{pmatrix} \text{Regime-survival pressure } (P_S^A \uparrow) \\ \text{Higher inferred capacity } (\mu(S, y) \uparrow) \end{pmatrix} \longrightarrow \text{Military escalation}\]
In democracies, security attacks operate primarily through the informational channel: \[\text{Security targeting} \longrightarrow \mu(S, y) \uparrow \longrightarrow M.\]
In autocracies, the same attack operates through both: \[\text{Security targeting} \longrightarrow \{P_S^A \uparrow, \, \mu_S \uparrow\} \longrightarrow M.\]

Proposition 2 (Regime Amplification) Holding constant the informational content of an attack and the relative costs and effectiveness of military force, security targeting has a larger marginal effect on military escalation in autocracies than in democracies when \(P_S^A > P_S^D\).

If response costs vary across regime types, this comparative result requires the difference in political pressure to be sufficiently large relative to differences in \(\Delta K^z\).



12 Terrorist Target Choice
Target selection cannot be treated as exogenous. Terrorist organizations choose whom to attack anticipating state responses. Let terrorist utility be: \[U_T(j, r \mid \theta, z) = B_j(\theta, z) - c_j(\theta) - q_j(r, \theta) + \omega V_j(r, z),\] where:

\(B_j(\theta, z)\) captures direct, symbolic, recruitment, publicity, or strategic benefits of attacking \(j\);
\(c_j(\theta)\) is the operational cost;
\(q_j(r, \theta)\) captures organizational losses inflicted by government response \(r\);
\(V_j(r, z)\) represents strategic benefits the organization receives from provoking state escalation;
\(\omega\) measures the weight placed on provocation benefits.

The organization anticipates the equilibrium response \(r^*(j, y, z)\). Its expected payoff is: \[U_T(j \mid \theta, z) = B_j(\theta, z) - c_j(\theta) + \sum_{y} \Pr(y \mid j, \theta) \left[ -q_j(r^*, \theta) + \omega V_j(r^*, z) \right].\]



13 A Separating Equilibrium
The informational mechanism is strongest when types have divergent targeting incentives. Define: \[\Delta c(\theta) = c_S(\theta) - c_C(\theta), \quad \text{with } \Delta c(L) > \Delta c(H).\]
Let \(\Delta R(\theta, z)\) denote the net strategic advantage of attacking a security target rather than a civilian target, excluding operational costs. A high-capacity organization selects \(S\) when: \[\Delta R(H, z) \ge \Delta c(H),\] while a low-capacity organization selects \(C\) when: \[\Delta R(L, z) < \Delta c(L).\]
When both conditions hold, there exists a separating equilibrium: \[j^*(H) = S \quad \text{and} \quad j^*(L) = C.\]
Security targeting then carries substantial information: weak organizations find imitation prohibitively costly.



14 Why Security Targeting Is Not Always Informative
If low-capacity organizations can easily target security personnel (e.g., exposed, unarmored patrols), \(\Pr(S \mid L)\) becomes substantial.
Under such circumstances, observing \(S\) provides little discriminatory information. This yields a pooling equilibrium: \[j^*(H) = j^*(L) = S \implies \mu(S) = \pi.\]
Security attacks can still trigger military escalation through the political mechanism (especially in autocracies), but the informational channel collapses. Hence, security targeting matters informationally only when operations discriminate by organizational capability.



15 Semi-Separating Behavior
Consider a semi-separating strategy where high-capacity groups always attack security targets, while low-capacity groups randomize: \[\sigma_H(S) = 1 \quad \text{and} \quad \sigma_L(S) = x, \quad x \in (0, 1).\]
After observing a security attack: \[\mu(S) = \frac{\pi}{\pi + (1 - \pi) x}, \quad \text{with } \frac{\partial \mu(S)}{\partial x} < 0.\]
As low-capacity imitation increases (\(x \to 1\)), the informational signal decays.

Proposition 3 (Target Hardness and Informational Content) The effect of security targeting through the informational channel increases with the degree to which the target distinguishes high-capacity from low-capacity organizations.




16 Repeated Attacks and Target-Specific Frequency
Let \(\pi_t = \Pr(\theta = H \mid \mathcal{H}_t)\) be the government’s belief after history \(\mathcal{H}_t\). Observing attack \((j_t, y_t)\) yields: \[\frac{\pi_{t+1}}{1 - \pi_{t+1}} = \left( \frac{\pi_t}{1 - \pi_t} \right) \times \left( \frac{\Pr(j_t, y_t \mid H)}{\Pr(j_t, y_t \mid L)} \right).\]
Over \(T\) informative attacks: \[\log \left( \frac{\pi_{T+1}}{1 - \pi_{T+1}} \right) = \log \left( \frac{\pi_1}{1 - \pi_1} \right) + \sum_{t=1}^T \log \left( \frac{\Pr(j_t, y_t \mid H)}{\Pr(j_t, y_t \mid L)} \right).\]
When operations are disproportionately difficult for low-capacity organizations to execute, repeated attacks provide cumulative evidence until: \[\pi_t \ge \bar{\mu}_j^z,\] triggering military escalation.



17 Numerical Illustration: Democracy Facing Only Security Attacks
Suppose a democracy has prior belief: \[\pi_0 = 0.20 \implies \text{Odds}_0 = \frac{0.20}{0.80} = 0.25.\]
Assume the likelihood ratio for attacking a hardened security facility is: \[\text{LR}_S = \frac{\Pr(S, y \mid H)}{\Pr(S, y \mid L)} = 3.0.\]

After Attack 1: \(\text{Odds}_1 = 0.25 \times 3 = 0.75 \implies \pi_1 = \frac{0.75}{1 + 0.75} \approx 0.429.\)
After Attack 2: \(\text{Odds}_2 = 0.75 \times 3 = 2.25 \implies \pi_2 = \frac{2.25}{1 + 2.25} \approx 0.692.\)

If the democracy’s threshold is \(\bar{\mu}_S^D = 0.60\): \[\pi_0 = 0.20 \longrightarrow \pi_1 \approx 0.429 \longrightarrow \pi_2 \approx 0.692 > \bar{\mu}_S^D.\]
Even with zero civilian attacks, the democracy militarizes because repeated security operations provide sufficient evidence of threat capability.



18 Political Pressure and Information Over Time
Bayesian updating exhibits diminishing marginal returns as beliefs approach certainty: \[\frac{\partial^2 \pi_t}{\partial n_S^2} < 0,\] where \(n_S\) denotes cumulative informative security attacks.
While the first successful attack against a hardened installation may fundamentally update beliefs, the tenth tells the state relatively little new about capability. Political pressure, by contrast, can accumulate monotonically with casualties, public embarrassment, and operational disruption:
\[\begin{aligned}
\text{Early attacks:} &\quad \text{Dominated by the informational channel} \\
\text{Persistent attacks:} &\quad \text{Dominated by accumulated political pressure}
\end{aligned}\]



19 Observable Implications


19.0.1 Democratic Civilian-Targeting Effect
Increasing civilian-target attack frequency increases the probability of military response more strongly in democracies than in autocracies: \[\frac{\partial \Pr(M)}{\partial n_C} \Bigg|_D > \frac{\partial \Pr(M)}{\partial n_C} \Bigg|_A.\]




19.0.2 Autocratic Security-Targeting Effect
Increasing security-target attack frequency increases the probability of military response more strongly in autocracies, conditional on comparable costs and effectiveness: \[\frac{\partial \Pr(M)}{\partial n_S} \Bigg|_A > \frac{\partial \Pr(M)}{\partial n_S} \Bigg|_D.\]




19.0.3 Cross-Regime Security Effect
Security targeting increases the probability of a military response across both regime types: \[\frac{\partial \Pr(M)}{\partial n_S} \Bigg|_D > 0 \quad \text{and} \quad \frac{\partial \Pr(M)}{\partial n_S} \Bigg|_A > 0.\]




19.0.4 Target-Hardness Effect
The escalation effect of security targeting increases with target hardness: \[\frac{\partial^2 \Pr(M)}{\partial n_S \partial h_S} > 0.\]




19.0.5 Operational-Success Effect
Successful attacks against difficult security targets produce larger increases in the probability of military escalation than unsuccessful or undemanding attacks.




19.0.6 Prior-Belief Effect
The informational effect of security targeting is greatest when prior uncertainty is high (\(|\pi - 0.5|\) is small), exhibiting diminishing returns as \(\pi \to 1\).





20 Conclusion and Explanatory Scope
The model’s core argument is that:
\[\text{Targets matter both because of whom they threaten and because of what attacking them reveals.}\]
The complete interaction can be summarized as:
\[\text{Target-specific behavior} \longrightarrow \begin{pmatrix} \text{Regime-specific political pressure} \\ \text{Bayesian learning about capacity} \end{pmatrix} \longrightarrow \text{Belief threshold crossed} \longrightarrow \text{Military escalation}\]
By untangling regime-contingent political accountability from cross-regime Bayesian belief updating, the theory explains why democracies can escalate against groups targeting only security forces, why autocracies react acutely to coercive infrastructure challenges, and why target hardness and repetition are pivotal determinants of state escalation.
